newsitem.title: GERMANY: More gains seen as Bund future hits contract high.
newsitem.headline: More gains seen as Bund future hits contract high.

text.p: Bund futures surged to contract highs on Thursday after U.S. employment data eased fears of wage-driven inflation and lifted global bond markets.
At 1408 GMT, the DTB Bund future was up 32 basis points at 102.37, hitting a new contract high of 102.41.
Traders said that although Bunds were likely to consolidate on Friday with the U.S. market closed, the contract should be able to climb further.
"There is positive sentiment coming from the U.S. That should give Bunds a push," said Timo Klein, analyst at MMS International.
Before the data, Bunds had traded in a narrow range just above psychological resistance at 102.00, shrugging off a fall in German May industrial orders of 0.8 percent from a month before.
The decline was slightly larger than some had expected, but not enough to encourage any fresh buying of German debt.
Bundesbank Chief Economist Otmar Issing, meanwhile, said in Frankfurt there was no sign of inflationary pressures in Germany and that there was no need for higher interest rates.
The benchmark 10-year Bund climbed to 102.93 from 102.55 on Wednesday to yield 5.60 percent.
Analysts said the jobs data also suggested that Treasuries should continue to outperform Bunds over the long-term.
One analyst, for example, said the spread between U.S. 10-year notes and Bunds could narrow to as little as 30 basis points by the end of the year from 86 basis points now.
Signs of a pickup in the German economy after a long period of sluggish growth could make Bunds less attractive relative to their U.S. counterparts, he said.
The jobs report also helped lead to further flattening of the German yield curve with the spread between two- and 10-year maturities narrowing four basis points to 218 basis points.
Bunds were little affected by comments from French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn that the public deficit there would be significantly higher than forecast.
Klein at MMS explained, however, that Bunds should benefit from talk out of Bonn and Paris that the two nations are having difficulty meeting EMU requirements.

That is because such talk leads to speculation of a broad monetary union which benefits debt markets in countries like Italy and Spain. Higher bond markets there tends to lift the entire European debt market boat, including Bunds, he said -- even if Bunds do underperform.
